title: We Owe Them More
author: Pondiscio, Robert
summary: Robert Pondiscio connects a memory of unexpected communal tenderness in Gramercy Park on the afternoon of September 11 to the decision, made months later, to leave journalism and become a New York City Teaching Fellow in a South Bronx classroom. He resists over-claiming causation between the two events, but argues that the day forced a question impossible to unhear afterward: not whether one will be remembered, but who one is responsible for and what one owes to people who have a claim on you. Pondiscio uses this personal history to make a broader argument, borrowing from Yuval Levin, that institutions like teaching are not platforms for personal performance but 'molds' that assign roles — parent, teacher, neighbor, citizen — carrying duties that exist independent of how the role-holder feels on a given day. The essay's central complaint, twenty-five years on, is that America kept its promise to remember the dead but not its accompanying promise, made by President Bush, to answer catastrophe with a durable sense of obligation to one another; Pondiscio reframes the teaching profession itself as one of the 'modest versions' of the duty first responders displayed in its most extreme form on that day.
points: Pondiscio traces his own decision to leave journalism for teaching to a New York City Teaching Fellows subway advertisement ('You remember your first-grade teacher's name. Who will remember yours?'), while explicitly declining to claim 9/11 directly caused the career change.

He reframes the day's lasting personal effect not as a question of being remembered, but as an inescapable set of questions: who are you responsible for, and what do you owe to people who have a claim on you.

Citing Yuval Levin, the essay argues institutions are not platforms for personal performance but 'molds' that assign roles (parent, teacher, neighbor, citizen) which carry duties independent of personal feeling.

Firefighters and police officers running toward people who were 'in their care' on 9/11 are presented as duty in its most extreme form, with ordinary daily obligations (including teaching one's students) framed as its 'more modest' everyday version.

Pondiscio argues America kept the first half of President Bush's post-9/11 promise (to remember) but not the second half (to answer catastrophe by living out a durable sense of obligation to one another).
quotes: The thing I remember-I will always remember it-was the eye contact. When adults saw each other, we stopped and looked each other full in the face. "How are you?" we asked.

The question was not really about being remembered. It was: Who are you responsible for? What are you doing with your time and energy that matters to someone besides yourself? Who has a claim on you? What do you owe?

I discovered how enormously difficult teaching is and how badly we prepare people to do it. Before long, I was writing again, this time about schools, curriculum, teaching, and what children need from the adults charged with educating them.

My colleague Yuval Levin has spent much of his career thinking and writing about the institutions of American life, and one of his most memorable insights is that institutions are not merely things that exist as platforms for our personal performance. At their best, they are molds that form us.

Police officers and other first responders ran toward people they did not know because those people were in their care. Duty was not an abstraction. It meant: Someone is depending on me, so I have to go.

We have become accustomed to describing what is owed to us and less likely to ask what we owe. We treat institutions as things to exploit when they serve our purposes and despise when they do not. The question cannot be: What is wrong with everyone else? It has to be: What is mine to take care of?
